title: RBAC v2 authz-lib API sketch (shared library) — interfaces, caching, call sites, test plan
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We have RBAC v2 types landing in control plane + console + admin tooling. We need ONE shared authz library that:
  - takes a request context (actor + org/project + scopes)
  - evaluates against the current policy bundle + role assignments
  - produces a decision object suitable for both error handling and audit logging
  - is consistent across Go services (control plane) and TS services (gateway/console backend).
- This is an implementation sketch. Not final API; intent is to converge quickly and then freeze it behind semver.

Non-goals (for first iteration)
- Not implementing identity provider mapping (SAML/SSO claims parsing) here, except to accept derived role_ids / principal.
- Not doing deep refactors of how services load org/project membership.
- Not covering data-plane inference token authorization beyond “tenant/project scoping” (handled elsewhere).

Inputs / assumptions
- RBAC v2 primitives:
  - resource: a typed identifier with scope (org/project) + optional concrete id (e.g., api_key_id)
  - action: a string from a controlled taxonomy (e.g., "org.api_keys.rotate")
  - scope: org, project, deployment, etc (current assumption: org + project are required for almost all control plane actions)
- Policy evaluation semantics per ADR-014 (please confirm before we lock the API):
  - allow-only semantics with explicit statements; if nothing matches => deny
  - optional explicit deny statements may exist; if so, deny overrides allow (needs reason code).
- Policy bundles are versioned (policy_version string) and can be updated at runtime (Hosted/Dedicated) or via signed artifact (Private).

Design goals
- Correctness: no more “forgot to add authz check” drift.
- Minimal overhead: authz check needs to be low-latency; use caching for policy + role resolution.
- Explainability: on deny, return reason codes that are stable enough for console UX + support debugging.
- Auditability: every decision can be logged with actor, resource/action, inputs (sanitized), policy_version, role_ids, decision_reason.
- Portability: Go and TS implementations should share structure so behavior is consistent; ideally share test vectors.

Proposed library surface (language-agnostic)

1) Core types
- Principal (aka actor)
  - principal_type: user | service_account | support | system
  - principal_id: string
  - org_id: string (required)
  - project_id: string (optional; include when relevant)
  - session_id / request_id: string
  - authentication_context: authn_method, mfa_present (optional)

- Resource
  - resource_type: org | project | api_key | billing | sso_config | dedicated_pool | private_bundle | audit_log | …
  - org_id: string
  - project_id: string (optional)
  - resource_id: string (optional)

- Action
  - action: string (taxonomy-controlled, e.g., "org.settings.update")

- Decision (returned from Evaluate)
  - allowed: bool
  - decision_reason: string enum (examples below)
  - matched_policy_rule_ids: list[string] (optional; can be empty on deny)
  - policy_version: string
  - role_ids: list[string]
  - evaluation_ms: number (or string formatted; see note)
  - cache_state: string enum (HIT/MISS/STALE) for policy + role resolution

NOTE: JSON schema constraint in logs: we’ll log numeric ms as a number in structured logs; in this sketch the library can expose both raw duration + formatted string depending on logging framework.

2) Reason codes (stable contract)
We need a small, consistent set so:
- console can show “You don’t have permission to do X” with actionable hint
- support can quickly understand what happened
- alerting can key off reason codes in shadow-deny mode

Proposed decision_reason enum:
- ALLOW_MATCHED_RULE
- DENY_NO_MATCHING_RULE
- DENY_EXPLICIT
- DENY_ORG_MISMATCH (resource org_id != principal org_id)
- DENY_PROJECT_MISMATCH
- DENY_MISSING_SCOPE (e.g., project_id required but not provided)
- DENY_ROLE_ASSIGNMENT_NOT_FOUND
- DENY_POLICY_UNAVAILABLE (fail-closed; should be rare)
- DENY_SUPPORT_IMPERSONATION_REQUIRED (user attempted support-only action without support session)
- DENY_BREAK_GLASS_REQUIRED (attempted incident action without elevated session)

3) Public API (Evaluate)
Signature (conceptual):
- Evaluate(principal, resource, action, context) -> Decision

Where context includes:
- request attributes for ABAC-ish conditions we already know we’ll need (but keep it tightly controlled):
  - ip_address (string)
  - region (string)
  - is_prod (bool)
  - support_session_id (string optional)
  - break_glass_session_id (string optional)
  - requested_fields (optional; for partial update endpoints)

We should be careful: if we let “context” become a dumping ground, policies get hard to reason about. Prefer defining named condition keys with docs + tests.

4) Convenience helpers
- Require(...) -> error (throws/returns standard error type)
- Middleware/Interceptor wrappers:
  - HTTP middleware (Go net/http + chi + grpc interceptors)
  - TS express/koa middleware

Error contract:
- always return 403 for authorization deny (not 404), except endpoints that intentionally hide existence (rare; needs explicit opt-in).
- response body for REST:
  - error_code: "AUTHZ_DENIED"
  - reason: decision_reason
  - required_permission: {action, resource_type} (stringified)
  - request_id


Caching approach

We have two different “things” to cache:
A) Policy bundle (policy rules)
B) Role assignments (principal -> role_ids; sometimes role bindings are per org + per project)

We should NOT cache per-request decision outcomes broadly because:
- inputs include resource_id and context; high cardinality
- risk of incorrect reuse
Instead, cache the underlying policy + bindings.

A) Policy bundle caching
- Key: org_id (+ environment) because private deployments may differ; also allow global default fallback.
- Value: parsed policy bundle + policy_version + loaded_at.
- TTL: 60s (Hosted) with event-driven invalidation; Private uses “bundle_version pinned” and updates on upgrade.
- Invalidation triggers:
  - policy bundle updated (global)
  - org overrides updated (if we support org-level overrides later)

Implementation notes:
- Provide an interface PolicyProvider:
  - GetPolicy(org_id) -> (bundle, version, source, err)
- Hosted: provider reads from policy service + local in-memory cache
- Private: provider reads from local signed artifact on disk (watch file / SIGHUP / installer hook)

B) Role assignment caching
- Key: (org_id, principal_id, principal_type) and optionally project_id if roles can be project-scoped.
- TTL: 30s (tentative) + explicit invalidation on role updates.
- Invalidation triggers:
  - role assignment write path emits event (org_id + principal_id)
  - gateway/control plane can also short-circuit invalidate on successful role assignment mutations

Implementation notes:
- Provide an interface RoleBindingProvider:
  - GetBindings(principal, scope) -> (role_ids, binding_version, err)
- binding_version is useful for debugging “stale binding” issues and for audit logs.

Metrics we want (align with PR_18477 direction)
- authz_eval_latency_ms (histogram)
- authz_policy_cache_hit (counter)
- authz_binding_cache_hit (counter)
- authz_denied_total labeled by action + reason_code
- shadow_deny_total labeled by action + reason_code (during dual-eval)

Security posture for cache
- Must fail closed if policy cannot be loaded and there’s no last-known-good (LKG).
- BUT if we have a recently loaded policy (LKG within e.g. 5m) and the policy source is temporarily unavailable, we can continue using LKG and mark cache_state=STALE + emit metric.
- For Private, policy source is local; treat read errors as DENY_POLICY_UNAVAILABLE.


Expected call sites (where library is invoked)

1) Control plane service (Go)
- Pattern: endpoint handlers call Require() with strongly typed resource/action.
- Example endpoints:
  - API key management: create/rotate/revoke/list (GitHub:redwood/pr_18480)
  - org settings, SSO config
  - model rollouts / deployment config
  - dedicated capacity pool config (GitHub:redwood/pr_18505)

Suggested enforcement location
- Prefer enforcement in service layer (not only gateway) because:
  - service-to-service calls exist
  - avoids “bypass” via internal clients
- Gateway can do coarse checks (tenant scoping, authn), but authorization should be authoritative in the service.

2) API gateway (TS)
- Use middleware for:
  - consistent 403 payload
  - attach decision context fields to request logs
  - shadow-mode dual-eval (v1 + v2) where needed

3) Console backend (TS)
- Guard “sensitive routes” in backend even if UI hides them.
- Provide a helper for “permission introspection”:
  - Can(actor, action, resource) -> bool (useful for UI gating)
  - But do not encourage using this for security; backend still requires Require().

4) Admin/support tooling
- Support impersonation and break-glass flows must go through the same library.
- Special principal_type=support with additional required conditions:
  - support_session_id present and valid
  - optionally ticket id / approval reference included in context


Go API sketch (rough)

package authz

type PrincipalType string
const (
  PrincipalUser PrincipalType = "user"
  PrincipalServiceAccount PrincipalType = "service_account"
  PrincipalSupport PrincipalType = "support"
  PrincipalSystem PrincipalType = "system"
)

type Principal struct {
  Type PrincipalType
  ID string
  OrgID string
  ProjectID string // optional
  RequestID string
  SessionID string
}

type Resource struct {
  Type string
  OrgID string
  ProjectID string
  ID string
}

type Context struct {
  IPAddress string
  Region string
  IsProd bool
  SupportSessionID string
  BreakGlassSessionID string
}

type Decision struct {
  Allowed bool
  Reason string
  PolicyVersion string
  RoleIDs []string
  MatchedRuleIDs []string
  EvalMS int64
  CacheState string
}

type Evaluator interface {
  Evaluate(ctx context.Context, p Principal, r Resource, action string, c Context) (Decision, error)
}

// Require returns *AuthzError on deny
func Require(ctx context.Context, e Evaluator, p Principal, r Resource, action string, c Context) error

// AuthzError should include Decision for audit log emission

type AuthzError struct {
  Decision Decision
}

func (e *AuthzError) Error() string

Notes:
- Evaluate returns (Decision, err). “err” is for system errors; denial is represented as Allowed=false with nil error OR as AuthzError from Require.
- Keep Evaluate side-effect free. Audit logging should happen in calling service using Decision.


TS API sketch (rough)

export type Principal = {
  type: 'user' | 'service_account' | 'support' | 'system'
  id: string
  orgId: string
  projectId?: string
  requestId: string
  sessionId?: string
}

export type Resource = {
  type: string
  orgId: string
  projectId?: string
  id?: string
}

export type AuthzContext = {
  ipAddress?: string
  region?: string
  isProd?: boolean
  supportSessionId?: string
  breakGlassSessionId?: string
}

export type Decision = {
  allowed: boolean
  reason: string
  policyVersion: string
  roleIds: string[]
  matchedRuleIds?: string[]
  evaluationMs: number
  cacheState: 'HIT' | 'MISS' | 'STALE'
}

export interface Evaluator {
  evaluate(p: Principal, r: Resource, action: string, c?: AuthzContext): Promise<Decision>
}

export class AuthzDeniedError extends Error {
  decision: Decision
  constructor(decision: Decision)
}

export async function requirePermission(e: Evaluator, p: Principal, r: Resource, action: string, c?: AuthzContext): Promise<void>


Policy evaluation internals (high level)
- Inputs:
  - role_ids (from binding provider)
  - policy rules (from policy provider)
- Evaluate checks:
  1) validate required scoping fields for the action/resource (e.g., org_id always required)
  2) compute effective permissions from role_ids:
     - for each role, expand rules
     - match {action, resource_type} + scope constraints (org/project)
     - match resource_id wildcards if supported (avoid initially)
  3) apply deny overrides if the policy format includes denies
  4) produce Decision with:
     - role_ids
     - policy_version
     - rule ids matched (on allow, optionally)

Open question: do we include matched_rule_ids in audit logs always? Might be too verbose but very useful for debugging in early rollout. Proposal: include on deny only in debug logs; include on allow only when sampled.


Testing / harness plan

We need confidence that:
- behavior is consistent across Go and TS
- new endpoints cannot ship without declaring a permission
- policy bundle changes don’t silently break critical workflows

1) Unit tests (library)
- Rule matching
- Scope matching (org vs project)
- Deny override semantics (if enabled)
- Reason codes for common failure modes
- Cache behavior: TTL, invalidation, stale-LKG behavior

2) Golden test vectors (cross-language)
- Maintain a shared set of JSON test vectors in rbac-policy-bundle repo:
  - inputs: principal, bindings, policy bundle, action/resource/context
  - expected: allowed + reason + matched role/rule ids (if deterministic)
- Run the same vectors against Go evaluator and TS evaluator in CI.

3) Integration tests (service-level)
- For control plane endpoints:
  - spin service with in-memory policy + bindings
  - verify endpoints return 403 with correct reason code + required_permission info
- For console backend:
  - verify sensitive routes enforce Require() even if UI would hide

4) Conformance / “endpoint must declare permission” enforcement
- Proposed approach (aligning with GitHub:redwood/pr_18633):
  - Add an annotation/decorator requirement for HTTP handlers.
  - CI linter enumerates routes and checks:
    - permission metadata exists
    - authz middleware is registered (gateway) OR Require() is called (service)
- Edge cases: health checks, public endpoints, webhooks. Provide explicit exemptions list.

5) Shadow-mode + migration safety tests
- Ensure dual-eval mode can compute v1 and v2 decisions side-by-side without changing response (except in enforcement mode).
- Metrics assertions:
  - shadow_deny metrics emit for mismatches
  - no PII in logged decision context


Operational considerations
- Logging
  - caller should log:
    - request_id, principal_id/type, org_id/project_id
    - action, resource_type + resource_id (if not sensitive)
    - decision.allowed + decision.reason + policy_version + role_ids
  - ensure we do not log secrets (API keys, tokens). resource_id logging must be reviewed per resource type.

- Performance budget
  - target: Evaluate P50 < 0.5ms in-process with cache HIT (excluding network)
  - cache MISS should be rare; on MISS, allow one network hop to policy/binding store (but prefer batch fetch).

- Private deployments
  - policy provider reads local signed artifact
  - need a clear story for version skew:
    - if service code expects action X but bundle doesn’t include it => deny + DENY_NO_MATCHING_RULE
    - this is safe but may break upgrades; installer should ensure bundle updated first or atomically.


Open questions / TODOs
- Do we allow resource_id-level grants in v0? (e.g., allow api_key:123 rotate but not others). My current vote: not in v0; too much complexity. Revisit after GA.
- How do we represent “list” vs “read” vs “export” actions to keep separation-of-duties clean? Need to align taxonomy (Linear:ENG-5383).
- Should evaluator support “explain” mode for debugging? (return matched rules, why others didn’t match). Useful but could leak policy structure; restrict to internal/admin only.
- Deny overrides: confirm we really want them in policy format; they complicate reasoning. If included, must be intentional and test-covered.
- Standardize required_permission in error response: do we include full {action, resource, scope} string or a stable short code?

Next steps
- Kaitlyn/Jordan: converge API names and reason codes; sync with audit logging spec owner (Kevin) so decision fields line up.
- Amara: confirm gateway middleware integration expectations + where to attach request_id.
- Leila: propose structure for shared golden vectors and CI wiring.
- Target: freeze v0 API surface by end of week after first working integration in control plane (so console + gateway can adopt without churn).
